Consult Summary:
- Acute progressive upper-lip swelling with dyspnea and dizziness ~30 minutes after prawn soup; suspected anaphylaxis. Emergency services activated; advised antihistamine while awaiting ambulance.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Ate prawn soup around 19:00; lip tingling/swelling began ~30 minutes later at left upper-lip corner, progressed to diffuse upper-lip swelling.
  - Symptoms worsening during call; reports difficulty breathing and feeling dizzy.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Throat tightness/dyspnea; unsure about chest tightness; dizziness.
  - No mention of rash/hives, wheeze, GI symptoms, or syncope.
- Pertinent negatives (if mentioned): None explicitly documented.
- Past medical history:
  - Asthma.
  - Peanut allergy; severe reaction in childhood requiring injection/hospitalization per mother.
  - Prior similar episode ~1 year ago after late-night Chinese food with swelling and breathing difficulty.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (albuterol) inhaler as needed; no maintenance (“brown”) inhaler.
  - Occasional antihistamines (unspecified); none on hand at start of call (mother later confirmed availability).
- Allergies:
  - Peanut; probable new shellfish (prawn) allergy.
- Social/preventive:
  - At home; initially alone, mother arrived during call and assisted with calling emergency services.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not obtained (telehealth).
- Observations/symptoms:
  - Patient reports progressive upper-lip swelling, dyspnea/throat tightness, and dizziness.
  - No documented visible rash or other exam findings.

Impression:
- Most likely: Anaphylaxis due to IgE-mediated shellfish (prawn) allergy.
  - Supported by: Onset within ~30 minutes of prawn ingestion; progressive lip angioedema; dyspnea/throat tightness and dizziness; history of atopy (asthma, peanut allergy); prior similar episode; clinician initiated emergency referral.
- Additional considerations:
  - Allergic angioedema without full anaphylaxis: less likely given respiratory symptoms and dizziness suggesting systemic involvement.
  - Contact urticaria/oral allergy syndrome: less likely due to progression and systemic symptoms.

Plan:
- Emergency management (during call):
  - Suspected anaphylaxis; ambulance arranged via 999. Patient advised to remain with mother while awaiting EMS.
  - Advised to take available antihistamine while awaiting ambulance.
- Follow-up (post-hospital):
  - Patient instructed to contact clinic after discharge; clinician indicated need to arrange “injections” (consistent with epinephrine autoinjector provision) and further management.
  - Counsel to avoid prawns/shellfish until evaluated (consistent with suspected trigger).

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  - Vitals; physical exam details (rash, wheeze, tongue swelling), full ROS (GI symptoms, syncope), exact antihistamine taken/dose, current possession of epinephrine autoinjector, comprehensive medication/allergy list, detailed asthma control, family history of angioedema, triggers, smoking status.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None noted.
● Transcript quality:
  - Telehealth urgent scenario; incomplete ROS/exam due to clinical urgency and ambulance activation. Some interruptions and unclear details.
